text: Historical European martial arts (HEMA) are martial arts of European origin, particularly those that were once practiced but have since died out or evolved into significantly different forms. While there is limited surviving documentation of classical antiquity martial arts such as Greek wrestling or gladiatorial combat, most dedicated technical treatises date to the late medieval and early modern periods, leading HEMA to focus primarily on the period from approximately 1300 to 1800. During this time, German, Italian, and Spanish schools flourished in the Late Middle Ages and Renaissance (14th to 16th centuries), followed by French, English, and Scottish fencing traditions in the 17th and 18th centuries. Martial arts from the 19th century, such as classical fencing and early hybrid styles like Bartitsu, are sometimes included in HEMA in a broader sense, as are traditional or folkloric styles from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, including folk wrestling and traditional stick-fighting methods. The term Western martial arts (WMA) is used in the United States and more broadly to include modern and traditional disciplines. In the Late Middle Ages, the longsword held a prominent position, and historical European swordsmanship (HES) is often used to refer specifically to swordsmanship techniques. The earliest known Western martial arts manual, Epitoma rei militaris, written in Latin by Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus between the 4th and 5th centuries, predates all other known Western martial arts manuals, except for fragmentary Greek wrestling instructions from Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 466. Medieval literature, such as Icelandic sagas, Eastern Roman Acritic songs, Digenes Akritas, and Middle High German epics, records specific martial deeds and military knowledge, and historical artwork like the Bayeux Tapestry, the Synopsis of Histories by John Skylitzes, and the Morgan Bible depicts combat and weaponry. Researchers have attempted to reconstruct older fighting methods such as Pankration, Eastern Roman hoplomachia, Viking swordsmanship, and gladiatorial combat using these sources and practical experimentation. The Royal Armouries Ms. I.33, also known as the "Walpurgis" or "Tower Fechtbuch," dated to around 1300, is the oldest surviving Fechtbuch, teaching sword and buckler combat. Johannes Liechtenauer is considered the central figure in late medieval German martial arts, though no manuscript by him survives; his teachings were first recorded in the late 14th-century Nürnberger Handschrift GNM 3227a. From the 15th to the 17th century, numerous Fechtbücher were produced, with several hundred extant, many of which describe techniques derived from Liechtenauer. His Zettel remains one of the most famous—though cryptic—pieces of European martial arts scholarship, with multiple translations and interpretations practiced worldwide. Multiple combat styles were taught simultaneously, including unarmed grappling (Kampfringen or abrazare), dagger (Degen or daga, often rondel), long knife (Messer), Dusack, half- or quarterstaff, polearms, longsword (Langesschwert, spada longa, spadone), and combat in plate armour (Harnischfechten or armazare), both on foot and on horseback. Important 15th-century German fencing masters include Sigmund Ringeck, Peter von Danzig (Cod. 44 A 8), Hans Talhoffer, and Paulus Kal, all of whom taught Liechtenauer’s methods. From the late 15th century, fencing "brotherhoods" (Fechtbruderschaften) emerged, notably the Brotherhood of St. Mark (attested 1474) and the Federfechter. An early Burgundian French treatise, Le jeu de la hache (The Play of the Axe), dates to around 1400. The first known master to write in Italian was Fiore dei Liberi, commissioned by the Marquis di Ferrara, who between 1407 and 1410 documented comprehensive fighting techniques in Flos Duellatorum, covering grappling, dagger, arming sword, longsword, pole-weapons, armoured combat, and mounted combat. The Italian school continued through Filippo Vadi (1482–1487) and Pietro Monte (1492, with Latin, Italian, and Spanish terms). Three early English swordplay texts exist before George Silver but are obscure and from uncertain dates, generally believed to belong to the latter half of the 15th century. In the 16th century, compendia of older Fechtbücher techniques were produced, including works by Paulus Hector Mair (1540s) and Joachim Meyer (1570s); Mair’s work is unmatched in scope and considered invaluable by scholars. In Germany, fencing developed sportive tendencies during the 16th century, with Mair and Meyer deriving from the Liechtenauer tradition but introducing new characteristics. The printed Fechtbuch of Jacob Sutor (1612) is one of the last in the German tradition. In Italy, the 16th century saw major changes, beginning with the treatises of Bolognese masters Antonio Manciolino and Achille Marozzo, who described variations of the eclectic knightly arts of the previous century, including transitions from sword and buckler to sword and dagger, sword alone to two-handed sword, and from polearms to wrestling (though absent in Manciolino), reflecting the versatility expected of martial artists. By the mid-16th century, polearms and companion weapons like the dagger and cape gradually disappeared from treatises. In 1553, Camillo Agrippa defined the prima, seconda, terza, and quarta guards (hand-positions), which became central to Italian fencing for the next century. From the late 16th century, Italian rapier fencing gained popularity across Europe, notably through Salvator Fabris’s treatise (1606). During the Baroque period, wrestling declined among the upper classes, seen as unrefined and rustic, and fencing styles adapted to new ideals of elegance and harmony. In Spain, La Verdadera Destreza ("the true art of swordsmanship") emerged based on Renaissance humanism and scientific principles, contrasting with medieval "vulgar" fencing; key masters include Jerónimo Sánchez de Carranza (d. 1600) and Luis Pacheco de Narváez (1600, 1632), with Girard Thibault (1630) a Dutch master influenced by these ideals. The French school of fencing originated in the 16th century, based on Italian traditions, and developed its own terminology, rules, and teaching systems during the Baroque period, with notable masters including Le Perche du Coudray (1635, 1676, teacher of Cyrano de Bergerac), Besnard (1653, teacher of Descartes), François Dancie (1623), and Philibert de la Touche (1670). In the 17th century, Italian swordsmanship was dominated by Salvator Fabris, whose De lo schermo overo scienza d'arme (1606) had great influence in Italy and nearly extinguished native German fencing traditions; later Italian masters include Nicoletto Giganti (1606), Ridolfo Capo Ferro (1610), Francesco Alfieri (1640), Francesco Antonio Marcelli (1686), and Bondi' di Mazo (1696). The Elizabethan and Jacobean eras produced English fencing writers such as George Silver (1599) and Joseph Swetnam (1617); the English verb "to fence" is first attested in Shakespeare’s Merry Wives of Windsor (1597). The French school originated in the 16th century, based on Italian traditions, and evolved into its classical form during the Baroque period. In the 18th century, during the late Baroque and Rococo periods, the French style of fencing with the small sword and later the foil (fleuret) emerged as a training weapon for small sword fencing. By 1715, the rapier had largely been replaced by the lighter and more manageable small sword across most of Europe, though treatments of the rapier continued in works by Donald McBane (1728), P. J. F. Girard (1736), and Domenico Angelo (1763). During this time, bare-knuckle boxing emerged as a popular sport in England and Ireland, with pioneers James Figg and Jack Broughton. Throughout the 18th century, the French school became the western European standard; Angelo, an Italian-born master teaching in England, published L'École des Armes in French in 1763, which was extremely successful and became a standard fencing manual for the following 50 years, including during the Napoleonic period. It was so influential that it was included under the heading of Éscrime in the Encyclopédie of Diderot. In the 19th century, Western martial arts split into modern sports like one-handed fencing and applications with military significance, such as close-quarter combat with the bayonet, use of the sabre and lance by cavalry, and cutlass by naval forces. The English longbow remains in use in archery. European combat sports of the 19th century include boxing in England, savate in France, and regional forms of wrestling such as Cumberland and Westmorland Wrestling, Lancashire Wrestling, and Cornish Wrestling. Fencing in the 19th century became a pure sport, with duels among the aristocracy becoming increasingly frowned upon and, when fought to the death, typically using pistols instead of bladed weapons. Stick fighting styles include walking-stick fighting (e.g., Irish bata or shillelagh, French la canne, English singlestick) and Bartitsu, an early hybrid of Eastern and Western schools popularized at the turn of the 20th century. Some European stick fighting styles trace direct teacher-student lineages from the 19th century, including Scottish and British Armed Services singlestick, la canne and bâton français, Portuguese jogo do pau, Italian Paranza or Bastone Siciliano, and Canarian juego del palo. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, the greatstick (pau/bâton/bastone) was used by Portuguese, French, and Italian military academies for exercise, recreation, and bayonet training preparation. A third category includes traditional "folk styles," mostly folk wrestling; Greco-Roman wrestling was a discipline at the first modern Olympic Games in 1896, with freestyle wrestling added in 1904. Attempts to reconstruct discontinued European combat traditions began in the late 19th century, led in England by Alfred Hutton, a soldier, writer, antiquarian, and swordsman. Hutton learned fencing at the school founded by Domenico Angelo. In 1862, he organized the Cameron Fencing Club in his Indian regiment and prepared his first work, a 12-page booklet entitled Swordsmanship. After returning from India in 1865, Hutton focused on studying and reviving older fencing systems, beginning to tutor students in "ancient swordplay" at a club attached to the London Rifle Brigade School of Arms in the 1880s. In 1889, he published Cold Steel: A Practical Treatise on the Sabre, which presented the historical method of military sabre use on foot, combining the 18th-century English backsword with the modern Italian duelling sabre. Hutton’s advocacy and practice included reconstructions of the systems of George Silver and Achille Marozzo. He conducted practical demonstrations with colleague Egerton Castle in the 1890s, both for military charities and to promote competitive fencing; exhibitions were held at the Bath Club and a fundraising event was arranged at Guy's Hospital. Among his acolytes were Egerton Castle, Captain Carl Thimm, Colonel Cyril Matthey, Captain Percy Rolt, Captain Ernest George Stenson Cooke, Captain Frank Herbert Whittow, Esme Beringer, Sir Frederick, and Walter Herries Pollock. Despite the revival and interest in late Victorian England, the practice declined after Hutton’s death in 1910. Interest in the physical application of historical fencing techniques remained dormant in the first half of the 20th century due to various factors. Similar academic work occurred in other European countries: in Germany, Karl Wassmannsdorf researched the German school and Gustav Hergsell reprinted three of Hans Talhoffer’s manuals; in France, the Academie D'Armes worked from 1880 to 1914; in Italy, Jacopo Gelli and Francesco Novati published a facsimile of Fiore dei Liberi’s Flos Duellatorum, and Giuseppe Cerri’s book on the Bastone drew inspiration from Achille Marozzo’s two-handed sword. Baron Leguina’s bibliography of Spanish swordsmanship remains a standard reference today. Starting in 1966, the Society for Creative Anachronism (SCA), an amateur medieval reenactment organization, renewed public interest in historical fighting arts and hosted tournaments using padded weapons to simulate medieval and Renaissance styles. The SCA divides its focus between Heavy Armored Fighting and adapted sport Rapier fencing, regularly hosting large re-creation scenarios worldwide. Their styles have been criticized for lacking historical authenticity, though many members engage in scholarly work. Academic researchers continued exploring HEMA from a scholarly perspective: in 1972, James Jackson published Three Elizabethan Manuals of Fence, reprinting works by George Silver, Giacomo di Grassi, and Vincentio Saviolo; in 1965, Martin Wierschin published a bibliography of German fencing manuals, along with a transcription of Codex Ringeck and a glossary of terms, leading to Hans-Peter Hils’ seminal work on Johannes Liechtenauer in 1985. During the mid-20th century, a small number of professional fight directors for film, theatre, and television—such as Arthur Wise, William Hobbs, and John Waller—studied historical combat treatises for fight choreography. In the 1980s and 1990s, Patri J. Pugliese began making photocopies of historical treatises available, greatly advancing research. In 1994, the Hammerterz Forum, a publication dedicated entirely to swordsmanship history, emerged. During the late 1990s, translations and interpretations of historical sources began appearing in print and online. Since the 1980s and 1990s, HEMA communities have emerged in Europe, North America, Australia, and the wider English-speaking world, attempting to reconstruct historical European martial arts using various training methods. While the focus is generally on martial arts of medieval and Renaissance masters, 19th- and early 20th-century martial arts teachers are also studied and reconstructed, including Edward William Barton-Wright, founder of Bartitsu; combat savate and stick fighting master Pierre Vigny; London-based boxer and fencer Rowland George Allanson-Winn; French journalist and self-defence enthusiast Jean Joseph-Renaud; and British quarterstaff expert Thomas McCarthy. Research into the rapier style of the Roman, Neapolitan, and Sicilian School of Fencing in 16th- and 17th-century Italy was pioneered by M° Francesco Lodà, PhD, founder of Accademia Romana d'Armi in Rome. This research focused on the Marcelli family of fencing masters and their pupils in Rome and abroad (e.g., Mattei, Villardita, Marescalchi, De Greszy, Terracusa), through publications of papers and books on rapier.

Historical European Martial Arts (HEMA) communities have developed in Europe, North America, Australia, and the wider English-speaking world, aiming to reconstruct historical European martial arts through various training methods. While the primary focus is on the martial arts of medieval and Renaissance masters, 19th- and early 20th-century instructors are also studied, including Edward William Barton-Wright, founder of Bartitsu; combat savate and stick fighting master Pierre Vigny; London-based boxer and fencer Rowland George Allanson-Winn; French journalist and self-defence enthusiast Jean Joseph-Renaud; and British quarterstaff expert Thomas McCarthy. Research into the rapier style of the Roman, Neapolitan, and Sicilian School of Fencing in 16th and 17th century Italy was initiated by M° Francesco Lodà, PhD, founder of Accademia Romana d'Armi in Rome, who studied the Marcelli family of fencing masters and their pupils such as Mattei, Villardita, Marescalchi, De Greszy, and Terracusa, as well as 16th and early 17th century masters like Agrippa, Cavalcabò, Paternoster, and D'Alessandri. The Accademia Romana d'Armi has also conducted ongoing research on Fiore de' Liberi's longsword system, publishing the first Italian analysis and transcription of MS. Par. Lat. 11269, Radaelli's military saber, MS. I.33 sword and buckler, and Liechtenauer's fencing tradition. Rob Runacres of England's Renaissance Sword Club has studied Italian sword forms and their influence on French styles since 2013. In Italy, Sala d'Arme Achille Marozzo investigates the Bolognese, medieval, and Florentine traditions, with Luca Cesari and Marco Rubboli focusing on medieval and Florentine traditions respectively, and Alessandro Battistini on the Florentine tradition. Central and Southern Italian traditions are studied by Accademia Romana d'Armi through Francesco Lodà’s work on Spetioli (Marche) and Pagano (Neaples). Tom Leoni (US) and Piermarco Terminiello (UK) have published annotated English translations of key 17th-century rapier treatises, including all of Fiore de' Liberi’s manuscripts, Manciolino’s Opera Nova, and Viggiani’s Lo Schermo. Ken Mondschein, a rare professional academic in the field, translated Camillo Agrippa’s 1553 treatise and the Paris manuscript of Fiore dei Liberi, and has authored several academic articles. Reinier van Noort researches Dutch martial traditions and also focuses on 17th-century German and French martial sources. The Germanic Langes Messer is studied notably by Jens Peter Kleinau and Martin Enzi, with Dierk Hagedorn publishing significant translations. Roland Warzecha leads research on Manuscript I.33’s fencing style at the Dimicator fencing school in Germany. Stephen Hand and Paul Wagner of Australia's Stoccata School of Defence study systems including George Silver, Royal Armouries' Manuscript I.33, large shield usage, Saviolo and Swetnam’s rapier, and Scottish Highland broadsword. Christian Henry Tobler is one of the earliest researchers on the German school of swordsmanship. Early publications include works by Terry Brown, John Clements, and David M. Cvet (self-published in 2001). In 2003, Stephen Hand edited SPADA, followed by a second volume in 2005, and since the mid-2000s, the rate of HEMA-related publications has greatly increased. Since 1998, Sala d'Arme Achille Marozzo has organized an annual HEMA championship in Italy, which was split into military weapons (autumn) and civil weapons (spring) in 2011 due to high participation, forming a larger coalition of Italian HEMA clubs. Civilian weapons include single sword, sword and cape, sword and dagger, and sword and Brocchiero (Buckler); military weapons include two-handed sword, spear, shield and spear, sword and targe, and sword and rotella. The civil weapons championship is one of the largest HEMA tournaments globally. Since 1999, HEMA groups have held the Western Martial Arts Workshop (WMAW) in the United States. In 2000, The Association for Renaissance Martial Arts (ARMA), formerly known as HACA, hosted the Inaugural Swordplay Symposium International, bringing together leading researchers from the US, Europe, and Australia. Since 2003, ARMA has held the ARMA International Gathering every two to three years. The Fiore-oriented Schola Saint George has hosted a Medieval Swordsmanship Symposium annually in the US since 2001. The annual Australian Historical Swordplay Convention, primarily a teaching event, was held from 1999 to 2006 in Brisbane (1999, 2006), Sydney (2000, 2004), Canberra (2001, 2005), Gold Coast (2003), and Melbourne (2004). Since 2009, Swordplay, a tournament event, has been held annually in Brisbane. Since 2002, Royal Arts Fencing Academy and the Rose & Gold foundation have hosted Ascalon Sword Festival, one of the largest HEMA tournaments in the US, which originally was part of the Arnold Sports Festival as the Arnold Fencing Classic. Since 2004, FightCamp has been running and is organized by London-based Schola Gladiatoria. Since 2006, Swordfish, an annual event in Gothenburg, Sweden, hosted by the Gothenburg Historical Fencing School (GHFS), has become one of the biggest HEMA tournaments worldwide and is considered the "world cup of HEMA." Since 2006, Nordschlag, an annual event in Edmonton, Alberta, hosted by The Academy of European Swordsmanship (AES), is Canada’s first interprovincial and largest Canadian HEMA tournament, with participants from across Western Canada and a full-day workshop featuring international and local instructors. Since 2010, the Pacific Northwest HEMA Gathering has been hosted by multiple schools and clubs in the region, featuring longsword, singlestick, glima, and a rotating weapon, with the location changing annually between Fort Casey and Pacific Lutheran University. Since 2011, the Vancouver International Swordplay Symposium has been held biannually in Vancouver, Canada, hosted by Academie Duello, bringing together instructors, authors, and researchers for workshops, lectures, and seminars. Since 2012, SoCal Sword Fight has been hosted annually in Southern California, including tournaments and classes in various historical weapons, with 329 registered fighters and over 500 participants in February 2023. Since 2013, Fechtschule Edinburgh, focusing on 16th-century fencing, has been hosted annually in Edinburgh, UK, by Stork's Beak: School of Historical Swordplay, attracting practitioners worldwide. Since 2014, the Purpleheart Armoury Open has been held in Houston, TX, formerly known as Fechtshule America, and is one of the largest and fastest-growing HEMA competitions in North America. In 2015, Australia's Stoccata School of Defence revived the World Broadsword Championship in Sydney, Australia, a tradition that was last won by Parker in Sydney in 1891 and was never challenged; Paul Wagner of Sydney won the 2015 event, also holding the Glorianna Cup, and Lewis Hand of Hobart won the junior title. The championship is held in the hometown of the current champion, so the next one will take place in Sydney in early 2017. Jousting tournaments have become more common, with events organized by Arne Koets, including The Grand Tournament of Sankt Wendel and The Grand Tournament at Schaffhausen. Sparring camps or fight camps are becoming more common, often being more casual than tournaments, emphasizing classes and sparring over formal competition. In 1998, the British Federation for Historical Swordplay was established as an umbrella organization for UK groups. In 2001, the Historical European Martial Arts Coalition (HEMAC) was formed as an umbrella organization for European groups with four stated goals. In 2003, the Australian Historical Swordplay Federation became the umbrella organization for Australian groups. In 2010, dozens of HEMA schools and clubs worldwide united under the HEMA Alliance, a US-based federation dedicated to developing and sharing HEMA, providing support in instructor certification, insurance, and equipment development. In 2012, Ruth García Navarro and Mariana López Rodríguez founded Esfinges, an umbrella affinity group for women in or interested in HEMA, aiming to encourage greater participation of underrepresented genders and support existing practitioners.
